chapters.title: Chapter 3: Debt Markets and Interest Rates

lessons.title: Bonds, Commercial Paper and Bank Loans: How Companies Borrow

children.text: Equity gets the headlines, but debt is where most corporate money actually comes from. Indian companies borrow far more than they raise from shareholders, and the terms of that borrowing quietly shape budgets, hiring plans and how hard your finance team pushes on collections. This lesson covers the full borrowing menu and the vocabulary that comes with it.

body.text: Debt is rented money. The rent is fixed, it is due whether or not business is good, and if you stop paying, the lender can take the assets you pledged. That single asymmetry explains almost every rule, covenant and credit rating that follows.

children.text: The Borrowing Menu

cells: Buying inputs before you have to pay for them
A structured top-up when the revolving limit is not enough
Short-term needs, for well-rated borrowers only
Mutual funds, insurers, pension funds, sometimes retail
Large, long-term funding at a fixed coupon
Foreign currency funding, under RBI rules, usually with currency risk

body.text: Trade credit sits at the top of that list for a reason: every company borrows from its suppliers before it borrows from a bank. If procurement negotiates 60 day payment terms instead of 30, the company has effectively raised a month of interest-free funding. This is why payment terms are a finance decision, not just a purchasing one.

children.text: The Supplier Credit That Is Not Actually Free

A vendor offers you a 2% discount if you pay within 10 days, otherwise the full amount is due in 30 days. Taking the extra 20 days feels free. Price it properly and it is one of the most expensive borrowings on the list.

body.caption: The true cost of skipping an early payment discount, expressed as an annual interest rate.

body.title: Price the Vendor's Offer
body.prompt: A supplier offers 2% off if you pay in 10 days, with the full amount due in 30 days. What is the approximate annualised cost of skipping the discount and paying on day 30, in %?
body.explanation: 2 ÷ 98 = 2.04% for the 20 extra days. Annualised: 2.04% × (365 ÷ 20) = about 37%. Your bank would lend at a fraction of that. Whenever a company is short of cash and starts skipping supplier discounts, it is quietly borrowing at credit card rates without anyone recording it as debt.

children.text: Bonds: The Vocabulary That Unlocks the News

markDefs.definition: A tradable loan. The issuer borrows a fixed amount, pays periodic interest called the coupon, and repays the principal at maturity.
The fixed interest rate a bond pays on its face value, set when the bond is issued and unchanged for its life.
The return an investor actually earns at the current market price, which moves inversely to the price and changes daily even though the coupon does not.

children.text: A
bond
is a loan chopped into tradable pieces. A bank loan stays with the bank; a bond can be sold to somebody else tomorrow. It pays a fixed
coupon
on its face value, but because the bond itself trades, the
yield
an investor earns depends on the price they paid for it.

stats.label: Face Value
stats.context: Repaid at maturity, whatever happens to the price meanwhile

stats.label: Coupon
stats.context: ₹80 a year, fixed for the life of the bond

body.caption: The coupon never changes. The yield changes every time the price moves.

body.title: Same Bond, Same ₹80 Coupon, Different Prices

body.text: Bond prices and yields always move in opposite directions. When you read that "bond yields hardened" or "the 10-year yield rose", it means bond prices fell and borrowing has become more expensive for everyone, including your company. It is not good news dressed up in technical language.

body.title: Which Way Did It Move?
body.question: You hold a bond with a ₹1,000 face value and an 8% coupon. Interest rates in the economy rise sharply, and newly issued bonds now offer 9%. What happens to the market price of your bond?
options: It rises, because your bond is now more valuable
It falls, because buyers can get a better coupon elsewhere
It stays at ₹1,000, because the face value is fixed
It depends only on the company's profits
body.explanation: Nobody will pay ₹1,000 for ₹80 a year when ₹1,000 buys ₹90 a year elsewhere. The price falls until the yield on your bond is competitive. Hold it to maturity and you still get ₹1,000 back, but sell early and you take the loss. This is exactly why debt mutual fund NAVs dip when interest rates rise.

children.text: Why Companies Mix Their Borrowings

body.title: Debt Mix of a Mid-Sized Indian Manufacturer (Illustrative)

columns.label: Borrowing From a Bank
points: One lender to negotiate with, and terms can be renegotiated
Usually secured against specific assets, with a charge registered
Rate often floats with a benchmark, so your cost changes during the loan
Available to companies of all sizes, including unrated ones
Monitoring is continuous, with stock statements and covenant checks

columns.label: Issuing Bonds or NCDs
points: Many lenders, so renegotiating terms later is far harder
Can be secured or unsecured, depending on the issuer's standing
Coupon usually fixed for the full tenor, giving cost certainty
Realistically needs a credit rating and reasonable size to attract buyers
Disclosure is public, so a struggling issuer cannot hide from the market

body.label: Why Not Just Use the Cheapest Source
body.context: Commercial paper is cheap until the day mutual funds stop buying it, as NBFCs discovered in 2018. Companies keep bank limits open precisely so that one market closing does not stop the business.

body.title: Four Months, ₹50 Crore
body.scenario: You sit in the finance function of a well-rated listed company that needs ₹50 crore for four months, to fund a seasonal inventory build. Treasury can issue commercial paper at about 7.5% a year, or draw down the existing cash credit limit at about 9.5% a year. The CFO asks for a recommendation.
body.prompt: Work out the cost difference and lay out what else should decide this, beyond the rate.
body.modelAnswer: On pure cost, commercial paper wins. ₹50 crore at 7.5% for four months is ₹50 crore × 7.5% × 4/12 = ₹1.25 crore. The cash credit route at 9.5% costs ₹50 crore × 9.5% × 4/12 = about ₹1.58 crore. The saving is roughly ₹33 lakh, which is real money for four months of funding. Four things should still temper the answer. First, commercial paper has to be repaid in full on a fixed date, while cash credit is revolving, so if collections slip by three weeks the CP still matures and you need a backup line anyway. Second, CP issuance depends on a good short-term credit rating and on mutual funds being willing buyers that week, which is not guaranteed in a stressed market. Third, issuance costs, rating fees and arranger charges narrow the gap slightly, so compare all-in cost rather than headline rates. Fourth, drawing down the cash credit limit keeps the banking relationship active, which matters when you need a sanction increase later. The common answer in practice is to use CP for the predictable core of the requirement while keeping the bank limit undrawn as the safety net, rather than treating it as an either-or choice.

body.title: Security, Covenants and What Actually Happens on Default

children.text: Lenders do not rely on goodwill. Three mechanisms protect them, and each one shows up in how your company is run:
Security.

A charge is registered over specific assets, often land and machinery for term loans, and inventory and receivables for working capital. That is why banks ask for monthly stock statements: they are tracking their own collateral.
Covenants.

Contractual promises about financial ratios and behaviour, such as keeping debt below a multiple of profits or not taking fresh loans without consent. Breaching one can make the whole loan repayable immediately, even if no payment has been missed.
Escalation.

Overdue accounts are flagged early by the bank, classified as a non-performing asset once dues stay unpaid beyond the prescribed period, and in serious cases the matter can end up in insolvency proceedings, where control of the company passes out of the promoter's hands.

For non finance managers this explains a lot of otherwise puzzling behaviour: why finance chases a single delayed customer payment at quarter end, why capex gets deferred abruptly, and why the treasury team cares about ratios that look academic from the outside.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: Short-term unsecured borrowing by a well-rated company, typically for tenors under one year and bought largely by mutual funds, is called commercial ___.
body.explanation: Commercial paper is unsecured, so it is available only to borrowers the market trusts. That trust can disappear quickly, which is why companies keep bank limits open as a backup.

body.title: Five Questions to Ask About Your Own Company's Debt
steps: How much of our borrowing is short-term and needs refinancing within a year
Is our interest rate fixed, or does it float with a benchmark that RBI can move
What assets are pledged, and which covenants are closest to being breached
Do we borrow in foreign currency, and if so is the currency risk hedged
If our cheapest funding source closed tomorrow, what is the backup and what would it cost

cards.definition: The fixed interest rate a bond pays on its face value, unchanged for the bond's life.
The return an investor actually earns at today's market price. It moves inversely to the bond price.
The length of time until the borrowing matures and the principal must be repaid.
Non-convertible debenture: a corporate bond that stays debt and never converts into shares.
Short-term unsecured borrowing by well-rated companies, usually for under a year.
A contractual condition in a loan agreement, often a financial ratio, whose breach can make the loan immediately repayable.
Secured debt has a charge over specific assets the lender can enforce. Unsecured debt relies only on the borrower's standing.
The risk that a maturing borrowing cannot be replaced on acceptable terms, or at all, when it falls due.

points: Companies borrow along a menu that runs from supplier credit and bank limits to commercial paper, bonds and foreign currency loans
Trade credit is the first form of borrowing every company uses, and skipping an early payment discount can cost the equivalent of about 37% a year
A bond is a tradable loan: the coupon is fixed for life, but the yield changes every time the market price moves
Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions, so rising yields mean falling prices and costlier borrowing for everyone
Bank loans are negotiable and usually secured, while bonds give cost certainty but need a rating, scale and public disclosure
Companies deliberately keep several borrowing channels open, because the cheapest one can close without warning
Security, covenants and the escalation process explain much of what finance teams do, from chasing receivables to deferring capex

All rates, tenors, debt mixes and figures used are illustrative teaching examples, not current market levels. Regulatory definitions and classification norms are set by RBI and SEBI and change over time.
